nameStory: The 'silky' in silky dogwood refers to the fine, soft hairs that cover the undersides of its leaves, giving them a distinctly silky texture when you run your fingers across them. This velvety feel sets it apart from other dogwoods and makes it easy to identify with just a gentle touch. The name 'dogwood' itself comes from 'dag wood' - referring to the hard wood that was once carved into 'dags' or daggers.
description: Silky dogwood is a medium-sized shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall, forming dense thickets in wet areas. It's a native dogwood with oval leaves arranged in pairs along reddish stems, and clusters of small white flowers in late spring. The shrub produces blue-black berries in fall and has attractive reddish-purple fall color. Unlike the showy flowering dogwood tree, this is a understory shrub that prefers moist soil.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs with prominent curved veins running parallel to the leaf edges. The undersides feel distinctly silky and soft to the touch due to fine hairs, while the tops are smooth and dark green.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers clustered in flat-topped bunches about 2-3 inches across. Each tiny flower has four petals and appears in late spring to early summer, creating a frothy white display.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round berries that start white, then turn blue to blue-black in late summer. The berries have a slightly waxy feel and often persist into fall, attracting birds.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are distinctly reddish-brown to purplish-red, especially noticeable in winter and early spring. Older bark becomes grayish-brown with a smooth texture.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies through underground runners, creating thickets in wet areas. Multiple stems arise from the ground, giving it a shrubby, clumping appearance rather than a single-trunk form.

habitat: Silky dogwood thrives in wet soils along streams, pond edges, marshes, and wetland borders throughout New England. You'll often find it growing with other moisture-loving shrubs like elderberry and winterberry holly in low-lying areas. It tolerates seasonal flooding and is commonly found in the understory of wet woods or along drainage ditches.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with a reddish tint, and the silky undersides become apparent. Late spring brings clusters of small white flowers that buzz with pollinating insects.
seasonality.summer: Full green foliage shows off the characteristic silky leaf undersides, and white berries begin forming from spent flowers. The reddish stems are still visible through the leaves.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn beautiful shades of reddish-purple to wine red, while blue-black berries ripen and attract migrating birds. The colorful stems become more prominent as leaves drop.
seasonality.winter: Bare reddish-brown to purple stems create attractive winter interest, especially against snow. Old berry clusters may persist, and the multi-stemmed growth habit is clearly visible.

funFact: Silky dogwood was historically called 'kinnikinnick' by Native Americans, who mixed its inner bark with tobacco to create a smoking blend that was said to be milder and more aromatic than tobacco alone - the silky leaves weren't the only smooth part of this plant's story!
confusionNotes: Silky dogwood is most often confused with red osier dogwood, which also has reddish stems and white flower clusters. The key difference is touch: silky dogwood leaves feel soft and velvety underneath, while red osier dogwood leaves are smooth on both sides. Remember: 'silky' means silky to touch!
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this native shrub with the more famous flowering dogwood tree - they're related but very different plants. Silky dogwood also goes by several other names including 'red willow' and 'squawbush,' though it's not related to true willows and the 'squaw' terminology in plant names is now considered inappropriate by many botanists.
compareHints: Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety. Red osier dogwood grows in similar wet areas but has smooth leaves, while gray dogwood prefers drier sites and has white berries on red stalks. The silky texture is your foolproof field mark.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
